item.title: [7] Sequence-Derived Geometric Priors Enable Controllable Generation of Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

MANTA generates controllable IDP conformational ensembles from sequence-derived geometric priors and shows that prior estimation is the bottleneck, which is directly relevant to ensemble generation and conditioning, though it is a sequence-to-ensemble model with a graph-Laplacian decoder rather than a cofolding or experimental-data-steered approach.

Jang, W., Shin, W.-H.

Predicting heterogeneous conformational ensembles from sequence remains a central challenge for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Sequence-to-ensemble models often entangle geometric inference with coordinate generation, obscuring error sources and limiting control over ensemble properties. Here we introduce MANTA, a C-level framework that separates these stages. An encoder derives geometric priors from protein language-model representations, and a graph-Laplacian decoder converts these priors into conformational ensembles. On a homology-held-out test set, replacing predicted priors with reference-derived priors under the same decoder reduces the median absolute relative radius-of-gyration error from 8.78% to 1.89%, identifying geometric-prior estimation as the dominant bottleneck in MANTA. Across an external benchmark of 27 IDPs, MANTA generates broad, locally valid ensembles. Decoder controls modulate mean compactness and conformational breadth along partially separable axes, while compactness modulation alters motif exposure in tau and amyloid-{beta}. Meanwhile, -synuclein variants shift local exposure populations at nearly unchanged global size. MANTA provides a diagnostic and controllable framework for ensemble generation that captures both global dimensions and local conformational organization.

item.title: [8] Information Theory and Statistical Learning
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A chapter from the forthcoming third edition of Cover and Thomas that derives diffusion and score-based models from divergence measures more systematically than usual, which is exactly the textbook-style math underpinning your steering work.

Abbas El Gamal

arXiv:2605.02989v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This manuscript contains preprint of a chapter in the forthcoming third edition of Cover and Thomas's Elements of Information Theory, posted with permission from Wiley. For feedback, please contact abbas@ee.stanford.edu. Learning and information theory intersect in both model training and the characterization of fundamental performance limits. This manuscript provides a concise and accessible treatment of the first intersection, requiring only basic background in information theory and statistics at the senior undergraduate / first-year graduate level. End-of-chapter exercises make the material well suited for classroom use as well as self-study. The chapter focuses on the role of divergence measures in model training, with examples ranging from linear and logistic regression to autoregressive models, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and score-based models. In particular, the treatment of the generative diffusion model provides a more systematic and explicit derivation than is typical in the literature.

item.title: [8] Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Shows that pooling shallow samples from several cofolding models (Boltz-2, Protenix-v2 and others) with a confidence-free selector beats deep sampling of any single predictor on antibody-antigen docking, which bears directly on evaluating and selecting among cofolding outputs for your ensemble work.

Ullanat, V., Gupta, A., Li, R., Amengual-Rigo, P. et al.

Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

item.title: [7] RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Showing that a fixed, prompt-independent set of steering vectors recovers about 90% of RL post-training gains in diffusion transformers is a surprising result about what steering a pretrained generator can achieve, and it bears directly on cheap embedding- or activation-level steering of generative models.

Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara, Duen Horng Chau, Pinar Yanardag

arXiv:2611.26627v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

item.title: [7] Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A nonasymptotic Euler-discretization convergence theory for flow matching from non-Gaussian sources such as heavy-tailed and multimodal distributions speaks directly to flow-prior sampling guarantees you rely on.

Yuchen Zhou, Lili Zheng, Yuxin Chen, Gen Li

arXiv:2611.26407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.

item.title: [8] Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

It diagnoses why one-step flow-map posterior samplers lose variance and calibration and fixes it with a no-cost training-pair placement, which bears directly on fast posterior sampling for inverse problems like the experimental-data steering you do.

Luming Yang, Siqing Li, Haoxian Liu, Zhenyu Bu, Jiazheng Zhu, Alper Yilmaz

arXiv:2611.23616v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.

item.title: [8] Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Gives a non-path-space analysis showing reverse-diffusion score errors need not accumulate polynomially under a Poincaré inequality, a theory result that bears on how much to trust diffusion samplers in practice.

George Giapitzakis, Ankur Moitra, Andrej Risteski, Dhruv Rohatgi

arXiv:2611.23617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincar\'e constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

item.title: [8] Biases and Limits of AlphaFold Predictions for Non-Globular Proteins
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A multi-lab analysis of where AlphaFold predictions diverge from experimentally validated non-globular and disordered states speaks directly to your concerns about what structure predictors miss and how to evaluate them.

Maria Cristina Aspromonte (University of Padova, Italy;), Alexander M. Monzon (University of Padova, Italy;), Miguel A. Andrade-Navarro (Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany;), Oriol B\'arcenas (Universitat Aut\`onoma de Barcelona and IQAC-CSIC, Spain;), Viktor Bartosik (Masaryk University, Czech Republic;), Pau Bernad\'o (Centre de Biologie Structurale, Montpellier, France;), Juan Cort\'es (LAAS-CNRS, Universit\'e de Toulouse, France;), Zsuzsanna Dosztanyi (Universit\'e de Montpellier, France;), Gabor Erdos (E\"otv\"os Lor\'and University, Hungary;), Isabella C. Felli (University of Florence, Italy;), Helena Gradi\v{s}ar (National Institute of Chemistry, Ljubljana, Slovenia;), San Had\v{z}i (University of Ljubljana, Slovenia;), Tam\'as Heged\H{u}s (Semmelweis University, Hungary;), Khalil Joron (Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel;), Pavel Kaderavek (Masaryk University, Czech Republic;), Eitan Lerner (Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel;), Dirk Linke (University of Oslo, Norway;), Pablo Mier (Universidad Pablo de Olavide, Spain;), Ana Panteli\'c (University of Belgrade and IMGGE, Serbia;), Roberta Pierattelli (University of Florence, Italy;), Salvador Ventura (Universitat Aut\`onoma de Barcelona and IQAC-CSIC, Spain;), Marija Vidovi\'c (University of Belgrade and IMGGE, Serbia;), Metaxia Vlassi (National Center for Scientific Research DEMOKRITOS, Greece), Lukas Zidek (Masaryk University, Czech Republic;), Silvio C. E. Tosatto (University of Padova, Italy;)

arXiv:2611.24546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AlphaFold has transformed protein structure prediction, making structural models accessible across the life sciences. We explore experimentally validated cases of non-globular proteins to uncover where predictions diverge from biologically relevant structural states and how molecular context shapes these discrepancies, guiding a more informed interpretation of AlphaFold models.

item.title: [7] Inverse Design for Conditional Distribution Matching
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A plug-and-play inference-time guided-diffusion algorithm for matching a target conditional distribution rather than a point output is a new framing of guidance that could transfer to ensemble-level steering.

Ori Meidler, Shaul Tolkowsky, Or Zuk

arXiv:2605.09439v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative models are powerful tools for sampling from a learned distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$, and inverse-design methods invert this map to find an input $x$ that produces a desired point output $y^*$. However, many design goals are naturally distributional rather than pointwise, incorporating the inherent uncertainty of $Y$ and targeting a specific form for it, a task not addressed by standard inverse design. To address this issue we introduce Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM), a new inverse-design problem class in generative modeling: given a joint distribution $\mathcal{P}(X, Y)$ and a target distribution $\mathcal{G}(Y)$, find an input $x^*$ whose induced conditional distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X = x^*)$ matches $\mathcal{G}$. We formally define two variants: Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (CDMS) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (CDMO). To solve these problems, we propose MLGD-F (Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion with a Fast inner sampler), a plug-and-play inference-time algorithm that combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. By leveraging single-step conditional sampling, MLGD-F enables tractable gradient computation, making the estimation of $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$ both memory-efficient and computationally lightweight. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic benchmarks, structured image transformations, and generative editing optimization, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank supports.

item.title: [7] Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Provable polynomial-time recovery with a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler under a diffusion prior gives theory for the posterior-sampling inverse-problem setting underlying your data-steered generation, though only for sparse linear measurements.

Ivan Lee, Xingyu Xu, Yuejie Chi

arXiv:2611.24602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

item.title: [7] Crystal structure of the first de novo designed phosphotriesterase ZAPP-1
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Baker-lab crystal structures of an RFdiffusion3-designed phosphotriesterase show catalytic-residue flexibility and AlphaFold3 recapitulating induced-fit states, a useful experimental validation of the design pipeline and of what cofolding predicts.

Woodbury, S. M., Kim, D., Mendoza, J., Kang, A. et al.

Designing a de novo phosphotriesterase requires scaffolding a dinuclear metal center bound by six catalytic residues, including a post-translationally carbamylated lysine, in a pocket that must also bind a small, flexible organophosphate and orient it for hydrolysis. We recently met this challenge using RFdiffusion3 to design the first de novo phosphotriesterases, and biochemically characterized our first hit, ZAPP-1 [1]. Here we report two crystal structures of ZAPP-1 at 1.42 and 2.28 [A] resolution. The crystal structures are nearly identical to the design model scaffold (C RMSD = 0.69, 0.71, and 0.99 [A] for three copies across two independent crystals), and the higher-resolution crystal assembles the dinuclear Zn(II) site in the designed pocket with carbamylated K16. The catalytic residues are near the designed geometry but demonstrate flexibility across the structures, albeit mostly rotameric (C{beta} RMSD [≤] 0.8 [A] for both copies in form 1). AlphaFold3 predicts the designed catalytic conformation with substrate bound and the observed crystallographic deviations without it, suggesting an induced-fit mechanism upon substrate binding. Together with prior biochemical characterization, there is strong evidence that ZAPP-1 functions as designed, validating the high precision achievable with our RFdiffusion3 design pipeline, but the structures suggest that future design should better preorganize the active site. The ability to design experimentally accurate and increasingly sophisticated enzymes directly from the computer should enable a new future of programmable catalysis and chemistry.

item.title: [7] Beyond Linear Paths: Generalized Interpolation for Flow-Based Generative Modeling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Compares interpolation paths for flow-matching models of conformational ensembles (Trp-cage, alpha-synuclein) and gives an exact KL-rate relation explaining convergence, which bears directly on the flow-based ensemble generators you steer, though it is not about experimental-data guidance.

B E, N., Mondal, J.

Flow-based generative models learn to transform random noise into molecular conformations by following a prescribed interpolation path between the two. Straight-line (linear) interpolation is the usual choice, but it is only one of many possible paths. We compare four paths within a single affine framework, xt = tx+ {beta}tz : linear, trigonometric, spherical and a new operator-based path in which each degree of freedom follows its own schedule. Linear interpolation is a limiting case of both the operator-based and spherical paths. The operator-based path bends inside it (contracted), whereas the trigonometric and spherical paths bend outside it (expanded). We train the same Transformer velocity field with each path on a three-well potential, the mini-protein Trp-cage and the intrinsically disordered protein -synuclein. All four paths reproduce the reference distributions with comparable accuracy, but they get there differently. The trigonometric and spherical paths resolve conformational basins early and approach the reference smoothly. The operator-based path delays part of the transport, so some features stall or briefly diverge before converging sharply. An exact relation between the rate of change of the KL divergence and the alignment of the learned velocity with the score difference, together with closed-form moments of each path, explains these differences. The choice of interpolation path therefore controls how a flow model converges, not only where it ends.

item.title: [9] Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1s trunk-diffusion boundary
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

This probes the Boltz-1 trunk-to-diffusion boundary with linear probes and SAEs and tests steering by editing the trunk representation, finding that decodability does not imply causal control, which bears directly on your steering of Boltz-class models.

Piotr Jedryszek, Tongmeng Xie, Adam Winnifrith, Alexander Hasson, Weronika \'Slesak, George Wicks, Toby Winnifrith, Oliver M. Crook

arXiv:2608.11475v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure remains equally decodable, whereas sequence chemistry becomes much less linearly accessible. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model by editing the trunk's single representation. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive on the same proteins (held-out F1 =0.78) produces no measurable increase in strand content at any of the steered layers. Removing helix or coil directions does not remove that structure. Linear decodability therefore did not imply causal influence at the sites we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against SwissProt annotations than against DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists.

item.title: [8] tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

tmol is a GPU-native differentiable Rosetta energy function with batched whole-structure refinement and use as a reward for generative design, which is directly usable as a physics prior or guidance term when steering cofolding models, and it comes from the Baker and DiMaio groups.

Andrew Leaver-Fay, Kieran Didi, Jeff Flatten, Alex Ford, Guangfeng Zhou, Nathaniel Corley, Hahnbeom Park, Maxwell W. Kazman, Rafael I. Brent, Joseph Kleinhenz, Henry Solberg, Andrew M. Watkins, Brian Kuhlman, David Baker, Frank DiMaio

arXiv:2611.21857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

item.title: [8] Saturation mutagenesis and NMR of a fold switch reveal position-dependent deep learning performance
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

A saturation-mutagenesis NMR benchmark of the GA/GB fold switch tests whether AlphaFold2-based methods capture mutation-driven shifts between alternative states, which is exactly the question of whether cofolding models learn physics or memorize.

Felbinger, N., Carillo, K. J., Chen, Y., Orban, J. et al.

A predictive understanding of the properties of fold-switching or metamorphic proteins can provide insights into protein dynamics and energetics, and enable the design of complex protein functions and molecular machines. Recently developed deep learning modeling tools, including AlphaFold, have led to dramatic increases in structural modeling accuracy, but their performance for prediction of fold switching or point mutant effects is unclear. Here we used NMR to measure all substitutions at three key positions of the GA/GB fold switch that differentially adopt -helical (3), {beta}-grasp (4{beta}+), or unfolded states, generating a quantitative experimental benchmark for mutation-level fold switching. Using this dataset to assess and compare a panel of deep learning and physics-based modeling and design algorithms, we identified variable and position-dependent performance across methods. Some AlphaFold2-based algorithms were able to predict mutant effects at individual sites, indicating partial sensitivity to physical effects of residue substitutions. Additional comparisons of predictions with experimentally measured stability changes further highlighted position-dependent success and general challenges for predictive algorithms. Together, this study provides a rigorous new benchmark for mutation-induced fold switching and reveals the capabilities and limitations of current deep learning models, establishing a foundational baseline for facilitating the next generation of prediction tools.

item.title: [8] High-throughput prediction of peptide structural conformations
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

This benchmarks AF2 subsampling-based multi-conformation prediction on 557 peptides against NMR ensembles, directly probing how well AlphaFold-style models sample experimental conformational ensembles and where they fail.

Ille, A. M., Markosian, C., Burley, S. K., Whitford, P. C. et al.

Protein structure prediction via artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) approaches has sparked substantial research interest in structural biology. In recent work, AlphaFold2 (AF2) has been adapted for the prediction of multiple structural conformations, beyond static structures, by using multiple random seeds and subsampling the multiple sequence alignment (MSA). Research applying this specialized approach has focused on regular-sized proteins, while smaller peptides remain underexplored in this context. Here, we report AF2-based multi-conformation prediction and systematic analyses of a set of 557 peptides (10-40 residues in length) with corresponding nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) ensemble coordinates. We found that predicted ensembles varied in similarity to experimental coordinate data, with disulfide-rich peptides bearing somewhat closer resemblance whereas -helical peptides exhibited greater dissimilarity. Distinct correlations involving MSA depth were also observed. These results reveal notable capabilities of AF2-based multi-conformation prediction for peptides but also highlight considerable limitations, emphasizing the need for interpretation discretion and improved multi-conformation prediction approaches.

item.title: [7] An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Treating noise-unconditioned denoising as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density, with convergence, diversity and memorization-avoidance guarantees and penalty-guided generation, is relevant theory for what diffusion priors learn versus memorize and for guidance robustness.

Xinyu Zhou, Jiawei Zhang, Stephen J. Wright

arXiv:2611.22202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(m\sigma_{\min}^2/\tau)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $\tau$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.

item.title: [7] Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

This trains a score-based diffusion sampler for unnormalized targets across tempered distributions using importance-corrected self-training, which is a relevant sampling idea for Boltzmann-style ensemble generation.

Hoang-Viet Nguyen, Hai-Dang Dau, Alexandre H. Thi\'ery

arXiv:2611.23072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

item.title: [7] Towards Efficient Auto-Interpretability of Boltz-1 Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

This is an interpretability pipeline for Boltz-1 Pairformer sparse autoencoders with candidate descriptions tested in silico, useful context for what cofolding models represent and for embedding-level steering.

Piotr Jedryszek, Oliver M. Crook

arXiv:2608.27754v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. We postulate that a latent is useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report some practical innovations. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured LLM cost, while recovering over half of them. However, we notice that in our setup the LLM judge is heavily biased towards consistent residue identity and a simple filter that selects for features with high amino-acid identity precision outperforms the stability thresholding. This simpler method has the added benefit of requiring no extra SAE seeds but it remains uncertain if it reflects a genuinely useful heuristic or an limitation of the LLM judge.

item.title: [8] Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Spectral steering analyzes when guidance of frozen diffusion generators realizes structured edits using the remaining-sampler Jacobian, with inverse correction that improves inpainting, which speaks directly to inference-time steering with a frozen prior as in your platform.

Angelo Moroncelli, Alessandro Leanza, Loris Roveda

arXiv:2611.19572v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

item.title: [8] Information-theoretic Limits of Learning and Estimation
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

El Gamal and Raginsky's textbook-style draft on information-theoretic limits of learning and estimation (metric entropy, Fano, minimax bounds), destined to be chapters in Cover and Thomas, fits your interest in long expositions of the math underlying inference.

Abbas El Gamal, Maxim Raginsky

arXiv:2605.06710v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Information theory plays a central role in establishing fundamental limits on what any learning or estimation algorithm can -- and cannot -- achieve, regardless of computational power. This draft provides an introduction to these connections. We begin by introducing concentration inequalities along with the notions of covering and packing in metric spaces, and the associated concept of metric entropy. These tools are essential for our analysis. We then introduce the learning-theoretic framework and derive upper bounds on generalization error in terms of metric entropy, Rademacher complexity, and the VC dimension, as well as mutual information and relative entropy. Finally we discuss the minimax estimation framework and establish lower bounds on minimax risk using Fano's inequality, yielding bounds in terms of relative entropy and covering and packing numbers. A significantly revised and augmented version of this manuscript will appear as two chapters in the forthcoming third edition of Cover and Thomas's Elements of Information Theory. For questions, please contact abbas@ee.stanford.edu.

item.title: [8] Binding Entropy Can Be Predicted by Crystallographic Ensembles
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Wankowicz lab shows that qFit-style multiconformer crystallographic ensembles quantitatively predict binding entropies, which directly validates the ensemble modeling you work with.

Miller, C. A., Wankowicz, S. A.

Protein-ligand binding is governed by free energy, comprising both enthalpic and entropic contributions. Yet structural interpretations of binding thermodynamics have predominantly focused on enthalpic interactions, largely neglecting entropy because it is difficult to quantify from static structural models. Here, we developed multiconformer ensemble models to analyze high-resolution X-ray crystallography structures and estimate both protein and solvent conformational entropies. These ensemble models successfully predicted experimental binding entropies measured by isothermal titration calorimetry for over 70 protein-ligand pairs across 12 proteins, revealing a strong linear correlation. Protein entropy, estimated using crystallographic order parameters that capture both harmonic and anharmonic motion, correlates linearly with experimental binding entropy. Incorporating resolution-corrected differences in water-molecule counts substantially improves predictions, demonstrating that protein and solvent contributions must be considered jointly. Analysis of water-protein hydrogen bonding networks partially explains entropic differences across complexes. These results establish that crystallographic ensembles can quantify binding entropy, enabling explicit entropic considerations in structure-based studies of molecular recognition for both functional analysis and drug design.

item.title: [7] Architecture of a portal complex embedded in the poxvirus core
item.description:
Score 7/10 · Nature

A structure of the portal complex embedded in the poxvirus core is a striking molecular-machine architecture result, likely from cryo-EM, and worth a look as fun reading with some structural-methods interest.

Ye Hong, Shiyuan Liu, Keren Wang, Rui Liang et al.

item.title: [7] Flow Perturbation++: Multi-Step Unbiased Jacobian Estimation for High-Dimensional Boltzmann Sampling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Flow Perturbation++ gives unbiased low-variance Jacobian estimation for CNF-based SMC Boltzmann sampling and is demonstrated on all-atom Chignolin, so it bears directly on equilibrium ensemble sampling with flow priors.

Xin Peng, Ang Gao

arXiv:2601.21177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The scalability of continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) for unbiased Boltzmann sampling remains limited in high-dimensional systems due to the cost of Jacobian-determinant evaluation, which requires $D$ backpropagation passes through the flow layers. Existing stochastic Jacobian estimators such as the Hutchinson trace estimator reduce computation but introduce bias, while the recently proposed Flow Perturbation method is unbiased yet suffers from high variance. We present \textbf{Flow Perturbation++}, a variance-reduced extension of Flow Perturbation that discretizes the probability-flow ODE and performs unbiased stepwise Jacobian estimation at each integration step. This multi-step construction retains the unbiasedness of Flow Perturbation while achieves substantially lower estimator variance. Integrated into a Sequential Monte Carlo framework, Flow Perturbation++ achieves significantly improved equilibrium sampling on a 1000D Gaussian Mixture Model and the all-atom Chignolin protein compared with Hutchinson-based and single-step Flow Perturbation baselines.

item.title: [7] The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

This shows that closed-form empirical flow couplings become nearly independent pairings in high dimension, with the drift energy scaling as log N / d, which is a clear theory result on flow matching that changes what is worth trying.

Tobias H\"oppe, Stefan Bauer, Qiang Liu, Andrea Dittadi, Kirill Neklyudov

arXiv:2611.21119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

item.title: [7] Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

This layer-wise probing of OpenFold's Evoformer, showing two distinct stages of geometric refinement and triangle-inequality violations, is a mechanistic analysis of how structure predictors compute, which fits your interest in what these models learn.

Ishan Khire, Naren Manikandan, Tyler Hayes, Giri Krishnan

arXiv:2611.19016v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_\alpha$-C$_\alpha$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.

item.title: [7] Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Diffusion Tree Sampling adapted to crystal generative models, with existing classifier-free-guided models as proposals and multi-objective Pareto sampling, is directly relevant inference-time steering, but it applies an established method (DTS) to a new domain, so it is capped near 7.

Daniel T. Levy, Vineet Jain, Tara Akhound-Sadegh, S\'ekou-Oumar Kaba, Siamak Ravanbakhsh

arXiv:2611.17462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

item.title: [7] Flow Matching from Viewpoint of Proximal Operators
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

An exact proximal/denoiser form of the OT-CFM vector field with Lyapunov analysis of manifold stability is the kind of flow-matching theory that informs how guidance behaves near data manifolds.

Kenji Fukumizu, Wei Huang, Han Bao, Shuntuo Xu, Nisha Chandramoorthy

arXiv:2602.12683v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We discuss the dynamics of Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) under the manifold hypothesis, where the support of the target distribution is a low dimensional manifold. We first derive an exact proximal expression of the vector field, using an extended Brenier potential for the OT; the vector field can be expressed by a denoiser, which is presented as the proximal operator associated with the potential function. Based on this explicit proximal form of the vector field, we analyze the manifold stability for perturbations to initial points, using the Lyapunov exponents of the dynamics. By analyzing the local behavior with the tools in convex analysis, we show that the dynamics contract linearly in the perturbation of the normal directions to the manifold, while perturbations in the tangential directions are preserved; this implies the stability of the manifold structure to the perturbations. To justify the theoretical arguments on the population OT, we also establish the convergence of minibatch OT-CFM with neural network learning to population OT-CFM under regularity and stability assumptions, with rate exponents governed by the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support the predicted geometric behavior.

item.title: [7] Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Elliptic interpolant schedules and Zoloflow give provably near-optimal sampling for stochastic interpolants with an explicit dependence on target conditioning, a genuine theory result for flow/diffusion samplers you may use.

Cole Becker, Taylan Kargin, Kimia Hassibi, Asuman Ozdaglar, Pablo A. Parrilo

arXiv:2611.18542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $\kappa$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $\kappa \rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(\kappa, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

item.title: [7] Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

RFD4-Proteina unifies all-atom design with conformational flexibility and extrinsic constraint-guided search in one latent space, which is relevant to your guided-sampling work, though it is a design paper rather than steering with experimental data.

Corley, N., Didi, K., Kazman, M. W., Brent, R. I. et al.

Biomolecular design requires finding chemically and geometrically compatible arrangements of interacting atoms and molecules. The complexity of problems which can be tackled by deep learning design models is limited by both the molecular landscape they encompass and their ability to explore that landscape effectively. Here we introduce RFD4-Proteina, which addresses these limitations through intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning within a shared chemical and conformational latent space. The latent space encompasses standard and modified amino acids, sugars, DNA, and RNA, with force-field supervision favoring physically plausible atomic reconstructions. Within this space, intrinsic reasoning uses recurrent refinement to adaptively allocate computation, while extrinsic reasoning guides search with arbitrary constraints such as energetic or geometric criteria. Across in silico protein design benchmarks, RFD4-Proteina achieves higher design success rates at greater generation throughput than all previous methods evaluated, with further gains from conformational flexibility, recurrent refinement, and search. The same model performs equivalently to or better than state-of-the-art specialist methods for side-chain packing, sequence design, conformational sampling, and design refinement. We demonstrate the power and versatility of RFD4-Proteina experimentally by designing specific and cross-reactive binders to therapeutically relevant targets, recognizing phosphorylations, controlling glycosylation, and creating enzymes that catalyze both bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions, including a first proof-of-concept demonstration of a de novo designed enzyme for active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis. By unifying diverse chemistry, conformational flexibility, and scalable reasoning in a single physically grounded latent space, RFD4-Proteina expands the frontier of biomolecular design.
